result.summary: Mummius takes command of the Roman army and defeats the Achaeans at the Isthmus. Corinth is abandoned, sacked and burned, and Greece is reorganised under Roman control. Pausanias adds a contrast between Diaeus and the Athenian cavalry commander Callistratus.

scenes.title: Battle at the Isthmus
scenes.summary: Mummius takes command and the Achaeans, after an early success, are routed by Roman infantry and cavalry. Diaeus flees to Megalopolis.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans risk losing the war and the freedom of Greece.

scenes.title: Callistratus at the Asinarus
scenes.summary: Pausanias recalls how Callistratus saved the Athenian cavalry in Sicily and died fighting.
scenes.stakes: Callistratus gives his life to save his cavalry.

scenes.title: Death of Diaeus
scenes.summary: Diaeus warns Megalopolis, kills his wife and poisons himself.

scenes.title: Corinth sacked
scenes.summary: Corinth is emptied, then entered, burned and plundered by Mummius.
scenes.stakes: Corinth's people face death, enslavement and destruction.

scenes.title: Roman settlement of Greece
scenes.summary: Mummius disarms cities and ends democracies. Later the Romans relax the rules and set up a praetor of Achaia.
scenes.stakes: Greek self-government and property rights are lost.

notable_quotes.reason: Records the burning of Corinth in 146 BC.

analysis.text: Pausanias contrasts Diaeus' cowardice with Callistratus' self-sacrifice, judging leaders by their courage.
The passage describes the end of Greek independence in 146 BC and Rome's province-style control through Achaia.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says the spoils of Corinth given to Philopoemen were still at Pergamus in his day.

language_notes.text: Attalus was king of Pergamum, a Roman ally in Asia Minor; the Caicus is the river near that city.
A stade (stadium) was a Greek unit of about 600 feet, so 12 stades is roughly a mile and a half.
"Wedge-like attack" describes a compact, pointed infantry formation driving into the enemy line, and "took them in flank" means attacked from the side.
Refers to the Athenian disaster in Sicily in 413 BC, when Nicias and Demosthenes' army was destroyed at the Asinarus during its retreat from Syracuse.
Menalcidas was an earlier Achaean leader who, accused of treachery and greed, also killed himself by poison; Pausanias compares the two men.
Manumitted slaves are those freed by their masters; here freedmen who fought for the Achaeans were sold again.
Votive offerings are gifts dedicated to gods, such as statues and paintings, which Mummius carried off as plunder.
Chief-magistrates according to property qualifications means offices were open only to the wealthy, replacing popular democratic government.
Land over the borders means owning land outside one's own city's territory, which was forbidden.
A talent was a large weight of silver, a major sum of money; 100 talents was a heavy fine.
Dating by the Athenian Archon and the Olympiad was the standard Greek way of fixing a year; the 160th Olympiad is 140s BC.

context_notes.text: Mummius was the Roman consul who finished the Achaean War in 146 BC. Orestes headed an earlier Roman embassy to the Achaean League.
Diæus was the Achaean League's general. Megalopolis was a major Arcadian city, and the League's cause was collapsing.
Lucius Mummius was the Roman consul who defeated the Achaean League and destroyed Corinth in 146 BC.
Attalus was king of Pergamum, a Roman ally in Asia Minor; Pergamus is its city, where Pausanias saw the spoils.
Achaia became the Roman name for the province of Greece, taking its name from the defeated Achaean League.

literary_notes.text: The imagined alternative of a siege underscores Diæus' failure of nerve and the missed opportunity.
Pausanias contrasts Diæus' flight with Callistratus' courage, using the earlier hero to judge the Achaean leader.
Callistratus' deeds, saving his men and then returning to kill five before dying, portray him as a selfless commander.
Diaeus is portrayed through his final acts: killing his wife and poisoning himself, which Pausanias judges as cowardly and avaricious, like Menalcidas.
The victorious general hesitates before open gates, fearing a trap, before finally burning a city that offers no resistance.
Pausanias adds that a praetor is sent 'still', speaking from his own time and explaining a lasting name as a result of the conquest.
